title: Μῆνις
titleEn: The Wrath and the Plague — Iliad 1.1–100
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The poem opens by asking the goddess to sing of the wrath of Achilles, which cost the Achaeans countless lives, and dates it from the day Achilles and Agamemnon first quarrelled. It then goes back to the cause. Chryses, a priest of Apollo, comes to the Achaean ships to ransom his captive daughter; the army is for accepting, but Agamemnon drives him off with threats. The old man prays to Apollo, and the god comes down from Olympus and shoots plague into the camp for nine days. On the tenth, Achilles calls an assembly and proposes asking a seer. Calchas will speak only if Achilles swears to protect him, and then names the cause: Agamemnon's insult to the priest. Apollo will not relent until the girl goes home without ransom and a hecatomb is sent to Chryse.

sentences.t:
μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
οὐλομένην, ἣ μυρί’ Ἀχαιοῖς ἄλγε’ ἔθηκε,
sentences.tr:
mēnin aeide thea Pēlēïadeō Achilēos
oulomenēn, hē myri’ Achaiois alge’ ethēke,
sentences.l:
The wrath sing, goddess, of Peleus’-son Achilles,
the ruinous one, which countless pains on the Achaeans laid,
sentences.i: Goddess, sing the wrath of Peleus’ son Achilles, the ruinous wrath that laid countless pains on the Achaeans,
sentences.n: μῆνιν ‘wrath’ is the poem’s first word and its subject; it is the word for a lasting, god-sized anger, and returns at 1.75 in Calchas’ mouth for Apollo’s. ἄειδε is the present imperative of ἀείδω ‘sing’, and θεά is the Muse, not yet named. Πηληϊάδεω is a patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’, with the epic genitive -εω (= Attic -ου), sounded as one syllable. Ἀχιλῆος has single λ for the metre. οὐλομένην (‘ruinous’) picks μῆνιν up again at the start of line 2.

sentences.t:
πολλὰς δ’ ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς Ἄϊδι προΐαψεν
ἡρώων, αὐτοὺς δὲ ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν
οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι, Διὸς δ’ ἐτελείετο βουλή,
sentences.tr:
pollas d’ iphthimous psychas Aïdi proïapsen
hērōōn, autous de helōria teuche kynessin
oiōnoisi te pasi, Dios d’ eteleieto boulē,
sentences.l:
and many mighty souls to Hades it sent-forth
of heroes, and themselves prey it made for dogs
and for birds, all, and of Zeus the plan was being fulfilled,
sentences.i: it flung many mighty souls of heroes down to Hades and made the men themselves a prey for dogs and for every bird, and the plan of Zeus was being fulfilled,
sentences.n: The subject is still the wrath. ψυχάς ‘souls’ go to Hades, while αὐτούς ‘themselves’ are the bodies left on the field: for Homer the man is his body, and the soul is what survives him. Ἄϊδι is the dative of Ἄϊς, a by-form of Ἅιδης. τεῦχε is an unaugmented imperfect (Attic ἔτευχε), and you will see this constantly: Homer’s past tenses may drop the ἐ-. κύνεσσιν is the epic dative plural in -εσσι(ν). Διὸς δ’ ἐτελείετο βουλή is a formula; the Odyssey uses the same half-line.

sentences.t:
ἐξ οὗ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε
Ἀτρεΐδης τε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν καὶ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
sentences.tr:
ex hou dē ta prōta diastētēn erisante
Atreïdēs te anax andrōn kai dios Achilleus.
sentences.l:
from the time when first the two stood apart, having quarrelled,
Atreus’-son, lord of men, and heavenly Achilles.
sentences.i: from the time when the two first parted in strife, the son of Atreus, lord of men, and heavenly Achilles.
sentences.n: ἐξ οὗ ‘from the time when’ can hang on ἄειδε (‘sing, starting from when…’) or on ἐτελείετο; both readings go back to antiquity. διαστήτην and ἐρίσαντε are duals, the Greek number for a pair: ‘the two stood apart’, ‘having quarrelled’. Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’ stands for Agamemnon, who is not named until line 24. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’ are stock epithets, translated every time in the same way.

sentences.t: τίς τ’ ἄρ σφωε θεῶν ἔριδι ξυνέηκε μάχεσθαι;
sentences.tr: tis t’ ar sphōe theōn eridi xyneēke machesthai;
sentences.l: Who then of the gods brought the two together in strife to fight?
sentences.i: Which of the gods was it, then, that set these two to fight in strife?
sentences.n: τ’ ἄρ adds a note of lively enquiry: ‘who, then…?’. σφωε is the epic dual pronoun ‘the two of them’ (acc.). ξυνέηκε is the aorist of συνίημι ‘bring together’, with the old spelling ξυν- for συν- and the epic uncontracted -έηκε. ἔριδι, dative of ἔρις ‘strife’, says in what spirit they were brought together. The question opens the story proper, and the answer comes at once.

sentences.t: Λητοῦς καὶ Διὸς υἱός·
sentences.tr: Lētous kai Dios huios·
sentences.l: Of Leto and of Zeus the son;
sentences.i: The son of Leto and Zeus.
sentences.n: The answer is a riddle before it is a name: Apollo is identified by his parents, and named only at 1.14. Λητοῦς is the genitive of Λητώ, mother of Apollo and Artemis. The poet asks a question and answers it himself, and the story moves on from the answer.

sentences.t:
ὃ γὰρ βασιλῆϊ χολωθεὶς
νοῦσον ἀνὰ στρατὸν ὄρσε κακήν, ὀλέκοντο δὲ λαοί,
οὕνεκα τὸν Χρύσην ἠτίμασεν ἀρητῆρα
Ἀτρεΐδης·
sentences.tr:
ho gar basilēï cholōtheis
nouson ana straton orse kakēn, olekonto de laoi,
houneka ton Chrysēn ētimasen arētēra
Atreïdēs·
sentences.i: For he, in anger at the king, roused an evil sickness throughout the army, and the people were dying, because the son of Atreus had dishonoured Chryses, his priest.
sentences.n: ὃ γάρ ‘for he’: what looks like a relative or an article is in Homer often a pronoun, a pattern that recurs constantly. The edition prints it ὃ with a grave accent. βασιλῆϊ is the epic dative of βασιλεύς. ὄρσε, unaugmented aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’. τὸν Χρύσην: the article points, ‘that Chryses’. ἀρητήρ, from ἀράομαι ‘pray’, is ‘the one who prays’; the literal layer marks it ‘praying-priest’ to keep it apart from ἱερεύς ‘priest’ (1.23). The sentence holds back its subject, Ἀτρεΐδης, to the start of the next line.

sentences.t:
ὃ γὰρ ἦλθε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν
λυσόμενός τε θύγατρα φέρων τ’ ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα,
στέμματ’ ἔχων ἐν χερσὶν ἑκηβόλου Ἀπόλλωνος
χρυσέῳ ἀνὰ σκήπτρῳ,
sentences.tr:
ho gar ēlthe thoas epi nēas Achaiōn
lysomenos te thygatra pherōn t’ apereisi’ apoina,
stemmat’ echōn en chersin hekēbolou Apollōnos
chryseōi ana skēptrōi,
sentences.l:
For he came to the swift ships of the Achaeans
to ransom his daughter and bringing unstinted ransom,
the fillets holding in his hands of far-shooting Apollo
upon a golden sceptre,
sentences.i: For he had come to the swift ships of the Achaeans to win back his daughter, bringing an unstinted ransom, with the fillets of far-shooting Apollo in his hands on a golden sceptre,
sentences.n: λυσόμενος, future middle participle of λύω, expresses purpose: ‘to free for himself’, that is, to ransom. ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’, elided before ἄποινα ‘ransom’ (a plural noun). στέμματα are the woollen fillets of the god, which mark Chryses as a priest and a suppliant. ἑκηβόλος, Apollo’s epithet, is usually taken as ‘far-shooting’ (ἑκάς + βάλλω); another ancient view derived it from ἑκών ‘at will’. θοάς ‘swift’ is the stock epithet of ships.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίσσετο πάντας Ἀχαιούς,
Ἀτρεΐδα δὲ μάλιστα δύω, κοσμήτορε λαῶν·
sentences.tr:
kai lisseto pantas Achaious,
Atreïda de malista dyō, kosmētore laōn·
sentences.l:
and he begged all the Achaeans,
but most of all the two sons of Atreus, the two marshallers of the people:
sentences.i: and he begged all the Achaeans, and most of all the two sons of Atreus, marshals of the people:
sentences.n: λίσσετο is unaugmented (Attic ἐλίσσετο), ‘he begged, entreated’. Ἀτρεΐδα, δύω and κοσμήτορε are all duals: Agamemnon and Menelaus, the two sons of Atreus, as a pair. κοσμήτωρ λαῶν ‘marshaller of the people’, from κοσμέω ‘set in order’, is an epithet of commanders. The edition prints no quotation marks: the speech begins with the next line.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδαι τε καὶ ἄλλοι ἐϋκνήμιδες Ἀχαιοί,
ὑμῖν μὲν θεοὶ δοῖεν Ὀλύμπια δώματ’ ἔχοντες
ἐκπέρσαι Πριάμοιο πόλιν, εὖ δ’ οἴκαδ’ ἱκέσθαι·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdai te kai alloi eÿknēmides Achaioi,
hymin men theoi doien Olympia dōmat’ echontes
ekpersai Priamoio polin, eu d’ oikad’ hikesthai·
sentences.i: “Sons of Atreus, and you other well-greaved Achaeans, may the gods who hold the halls of Olympus grant you to sack the city of Priam and to come safely home;
sentences.n: δοῖεν is an aorist optative of wish, ‘may they grant’, with the infinitives ἐκπέρσαι ‘sack utterly’ and ἱκέσθαι ‘come’. ἐϋκνήμιδες ‘well-greaved’, the stock epithet of the Achaeans: greaves are the shin-guards. The edition prints the diaeresis (ἐϋ-). Πριάμοιο has the epic genitive -οιο (= Attic -ου). οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε ‘homeward’, with the suffix -δε of direction. Chryses opens with a blessing before he makes his request.

sentences.t:
παῖδα δ’ ἐμοὶ λύσαιτε φίλην, τὰ δ’ ἄποινα δέχεσθαι,
ἁζόμενοι Διὸς υἱὸν ἑκηβόλον Ἀπόλλωνα.
sentences.tr:
paida d’ emoi lysaite philēn, ta d’ apoina dechesthai,
hazomenoi Dios huion hekēbolon Apollōna.
sentences.l:
and my child release to me, my dear one, and the ransom accept,
revering the son of Zeus, far-shooting Apollo.”
sentences.i: but release my dear child to me and accept the ransom, in reverence for the son of Zeus, far-shooting Apollo.”
sentences.n: λύσαιτε is an optative of polite request, ‘would you release’. δέχεσθαι is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘accept’, a usage common in Homer. φίλην ‘dear’ stands apart from παῖδα, which it qualifies. ἁζόμενοι ‘revering, in awe of’ gives the ground of the request: the god behind the priest.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοι μὲν πάντες ἐπευφήμησαν Ἀχαιοὶ
αἰδεῖσθαί θ’ ἱερῆα καὶ ἀγλαὰ δέχθαι ἄποινα·
sentences.tr:
enth’ alloi men pantes epeuphēmēsan Achaioi
aideisthai th’ hierēa kai aglaa dechthai apoina·
sentences.l:
Then all the other Achaeans shouted-assent,
to respect the priest and to accept the splendid ransom;
sentences.i: Then all the other Achaeans cried out in favour of respecting the priest and accepting the splendid ransom;
sentences.n: ἐπευφήμησαν, from ἐπευφημέω, is to voice assent aloud. The two infinitives αἰδεῖσθαι ‘to respect’ and δέχθαι ‘to accept’ say what they called for. δέχθαι is an athematic aorist infinitive of δέχομαι, with no thematic vowel. ἱερῆα is the epic accusative of ἱερεύς ‘priest’. ἀγλαά ‘splendid’ is the house rendering of ἀγλαός, kept even where it sits oddly.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι ἥνδανε θυμῷ,
ἀλλὰ κακῶς ἀφίει, κρατερὸν δ’ ἐπὶ μῦθον ἔτελλε·
sentences.tr:
all’ ouk Atreïdēi Agamemnoni hēndane thymōi,
alla kakōs aphiei, krateron d’ epi mython etelle·
sentences.l:
but not to Atreus’ son Agamemnon was it pleasing in his heart,
but harshly he sent him away, and a strong word enjoined on him:
sentences.i: but it did not please the heart of Agamemnon, son of Atreus: he sent him off harshly and laid a strong charge on him.
sentences.n: ἥνδανε θυμῷ ‘was pleasing to his heart’: Ἀτρεΐδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονι is a dative of the person, and θυμῷ narrows it to his heart. Agamemnon is named here for the first time. ἀφίει is the unaugmented imperfect of ἀφίημι ‘send away’. ἐπὶ … ἔτελλε is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: ἐπιτέλλω ‘enjoin, lay a charge on’. κρατερός keeps the house rendering ‘strong’.

sentences.t:
μή σε γέρον κοίλῃσιν ἐγὼ παρὰ νηυσὶ κιχείω
ἢ νῦν δηθύνοντ’ ἢ ὕστερον αὖτις ἰόντα,
μή νύ τοι οὐ χραίσμῃ σκῆπτρον καὶ στέμμα θεοῖο·
sentences.tr:
mē se geron koilēisin egō para nēusi kicheiō
ē nyn dēthynont’ ē hysteron autis ionta,
mē ny toi ou chraismēi skēptron kai stemma theoio·
sentences.i: “Old man, let me not find you by the hollow ships, either loitering now or coming back again later, or the sceptre and the god’s fillet may be no help to you then.
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive κιχείω (epic aorist subjunctive of κιχάνω ‘come upon, find’) is a warning: ‘let me not find you’. κοίλῃσιν and νηυσί are epic datives plural, ‘hollow ships’. ἰόντα is the participle of εἶμι ‘go’. The second μή, with χραίσμῃ (aorist subjunctive of χραισμέω ‘help, avail’), is ‘lest’. νυ is an epic particle, ‘now, then’. The sceptre and fillet are those of 1.14–15.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐ λύσω·
sentences.tr: tēn d’ egō ou lysō·
sentences.l: Her I will not release;
sentences.i: Her I will not set free.
sentences.n: τήν is the article used as a pronoun, ‘her’, standing first for emphasis. λύσω is the future of λύω ‘release’, the verb Chryses used in his plea (λύσαιτε, 1.20); Agamemnon answers him in his own word.

sentences.t:
πρίν μιν καὶ γῆρας ἔπεισιν
ἡμετέρῳ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ ἐν Ἄργεϊ τηλόθι πάτρης
ἱστὸν ἐποιχομένην καὶ ἐμὸν λέχος ἀντιόωσαν·
sentences.tr:
prin min kai gēras epeisin
hēmeterōi eni oikōi en Argeï tēlothi patrēs
histon epoichomenēn kai emon lechos antioōsan·
sentences.i: before that, old age will come upon her in our house in Argos, far from her own country, as she plies the loom and comes to my bed.
sentences.n: πρίν here is an adverb, ‘sooner, before that’. ἔπεισιν is the future of ἔπειμι (from εἶμι ‘go’), ‘will come upon’. ἐνί is the epic form of ἐν. Ἄργεϊ is the dative of Ἄργος, here Agamemnon’s homeland in the Peloponnese. τηλόθι ‘far off’, with the genitive πάτρης, has the place-suffix -θι. ἀντιόωσαν (from ἀντιάω ‘meet, partake of’) has the epic lengthened vowel: she will come to his bed as his concubine, which is what he means.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴθι μή μ’ ἐρέθιζε σαώτερος ὥς κε νέηαι.
sentences.tr: all’ ithi mē m’ erethize saōteros hōs ke neēai.
sentences.l: But go, do not provoke me, safer so that you may return.”
sentences.i: Now go, and do not provoke me, so that you may get home the safer.”
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. μή with the present imperative ἐρέθιζε forbids what is under way: ‘stop provoking me’. ὥς κε with the subjunctive νέηαι (from νέομαι ‘return home’) is a purpose clause, ‘so that you may return’. σαώτερος, comparative of σάος ‘safe’, agrees with the subject: ‘the safer’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἔδεισεν δ’ ὃ γέρων καὶ ἐπείθετο μύθῳ·
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, edeisen d’ ho gerōn kai epeitheto mythōi·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and obeyed the word;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and did as he was told.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ is the standing formula that closes a speech. ὃ γέρων: the old pronoun is on its way to becoming the article, ‘he, the old man’. ἔδεισεν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’; its first syllable counts long because the δ that follows was once δϝ, a double consonant. ἐπείθετο μύθῳ ‘obeyed the word’, with the dative.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἀκέων παρὰ θῖνα πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr: bē d’ akeōn para thina polyphloisboio thalassēs·
sentences.l: And he went, silent, along the shore of the much-roaring sea;
sentences.i: He went without a word along the shore of the loud-roaring sea.
sentences.n: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω ‘go’ (= ἔβη). ἀκέων ‘in silence’ is an adverb, in origin a participle. πολυφλοίσβοιο θαλάσσης ‘the much-roaring sea’ is a line-end formula, taken over with its English from the Odyssey; φλοῖσβος is the roar of breaking surf. The old man’s silence on the noisy shore is set against the prayer that follows.

sentences.t:
πολλὰ δ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπάνευθε κιὼν ἠρᾶθ’ ὁ γεραιὸς
Ἀπόλλωνι ἄνακτι, τὸν ἠΰκομος τέκε Λητώ·
sentences.tr:
polla d’ epeit’ apaneuthe kiōn ērath’ ho geraios
Apollōni anakti, ton ēÿkomos teke Lētō·
sentences.l:
and much then, going apart, prayed the old man
to Apollo the lord, whom fine-haired Leto bore:
sentences.i: Then, when he had gone apart, the old man prayed long to lord Apollo, whom fine-haired Leto bore:
sentences.n: πολλά is adverbial, ‘much, earnestly’. κιών is a participle of a defective verb ‘go’. ἠρᾶθ’ is ἠρᾶτο, imperfect of ἀράομαι ‘pray’, the verb behind ἀρητήρ (1.11). γεραιός ‘old man’ varies γέρων. τόν is relative here, ‘whom’. ἠΰκομος ‘fine-haired’ is a stock epithet of goddesses; the edition prints the diaeresis (ἠΰ-).

sentences.t:
κλῦθί μευ ἀργυρότοξ’, ὃς Χρύσην ἀμφιβέβηκας
Κίλλαν τε ζαθέην Τενέδοιό τε ἶφι ἀνάσσεις,
sentences.tr:
klythi meu argyrotox’, hos Chrysēn amphibebēkas
Killan te zatheēn Tenedoio te iphi anasseis,
sentences.l:
“Hear me, silver-bowed one, who stand-over Chryse
and Cilla, most holy, and of Tenedos are lord with force,
sentences.i: “Hear me, silver-bowed one, you who stand guard over Chryse and most holy Cilla, and powerfully rule Tenedos:
sentences.n: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, with the genitive μευ (epic = μου). ἀργυρότοξ’ is the vocative ἀργυρότοξε ‘silver-bowed’, elided. ἀμφιβέβηκας, perfect of ἀμφιβαίνω, is to stand astride something to protect it. Χρύσην here is the town Chryse (Χρύση); at 1.11 the same form was the man Chryses (Χρύσης). ζαθέην ‘most holy’ has the intensive prefix ζα-. ἶφι is the old instrumental of ἴς ‘force’.

sentences.t:
Σμινθεῦ εἴ ποτέ τοι χαρίεντ’ ἐπὶ νηὸν ἔρεψα,
ἢ εἰ δή ποτέ τοι κατὰ πίονα μηρί’ ἔκηα
ταύρων ἠδ’ αἰγῶν, τὸ δέ μοι κρήηνον ἐέλδωρ·
sentences.tr:
Smintheu ei pote toi charient’ epi nēon erepsa,
ē ei dē pote toi kata piona mēri’ ekēa
taurōn ēd’ aigōn, to de moi krēēnon eeldōr·
sentences.l:
Smintheus, if ever for you a pleasing temple I roofed,
or if indeed ever for you fat thigh-pieces I burned
of bulls and of goats, this for me fulfil, the wish:
sentences.i: Smintheus, if ever I roofed a temple to please you, or if ever I burned the fat thigh-pieces of bulls and goats for you, fulfil this wish for me:
sentences.n: Σμινθεῦ is a cult title of Apollo, of uncertain meaning; the ancients tied it to a word for ‘mouse’ or to a place called Sminthe. The prayer reminds the god of past service. ἐπὶ … ἔρεψα (ἐπερέφω ‘roof over’) and κατὰ … ἔκηα (κατακαίω ‘burn up’) are both tmesis. κρήηνον, aorist imperative of κραιαίνω ‘fulfil’. τό is a pronoun, ‘this’, explained by ἐέλδωρ ‘wish’ at the line’s end.

sentences.t: τίσειαν Δαναοὶ ἐμὰ δάκρυα σοῖσι βέλεσσιν.
sentences.tr: tiseian Danaoi ema dakrya soisi belessin.
sentences.l: May the Danaans pay for my tears with your shafts.”
sentences.i: Let the Danaans pay for my tears under your arrows.”
sentences.n: τίσειαν, aorist optative of τίνω ‘pay, pay for’, states the wish itself. Δαναοί ‘Danaans’ is one of Homer’s three names for the besiegers, with Ἀχαιοί and Ἀργεῖοι; all three mean the same army. βέλεσσιν, the epic dative plural of βέλος ‘missile, shaft’. σοῖσι is the epic dative plural of σός ‘your’. The prayer ends on the weapon it asks for.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος, τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
βῆ δὲ κατ’ Οὐλύμποιο καρήνων χωόμενος κῆρ,
τόξ’ ὤμοισιν ἔχων ἀμφηρεφέα τε φαρέτρην·
sentences.tr:
hōs ephat’ euchomenos, tou d’ eklye Phoibos Apollōn,
bē de kat’ Oulympoio karēnōn chōomenos kēr,
tox’ ōmoisin echōn amphērephea te pharetrēn·
sentences.i: So he prayed, and Phoebus Apollo heard him, and came down from the peaks of Olympus, incensed at heart, with his bow on his shoulders and his close-lidded quiver.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ εὐχόμενος ‘so he spoke, praying’ closes a prayer, and τοῦ δ’ ἔκλυε ‘and him heard’ (κλύω + genitive) says it was answered; the Odyssey has the same line with other gods. Φοῖβος ‘bright’ is Apollo’s epithet. Οὐλύμποιο has the epic -οιο. χωόμενος κῆρ ‘incensed in heart’: κῆρ is an accusative of respect. ἀμφηρεφής is ‘covered over at both ends’, a closed quiver.

sentences.t:
ἔκλαγξαν δ’ ἄρ’ ὀϊστοὶ ἐπ’ ὤμων χωομένοιο,
αὐτοῦ κινηθέντος·
sentences.tr:
eklanxan d’ ar’ oïstoi ep’ ōmōn chōomenoio,
autou kinēthentos·
sentences.l:
And rang the arrows on the shoulders of the incensed one,
as he himself moved;
sentences.i: The arrows rattled on the shoulders of the incensed god as he moved;
sentences.n: ἔκλαγξαν is the aorist of κλάζω ‘ring, clang, scream’, a word for sharp sounds of birds and metal. ὀϊστοί ‘arrows’ is printed with the diaeresis. χωομένοιο agrees with the god whose shoulders they are, and αὐτοῦ κινηθέντος is a genitive absolute, ‘as he himself moved’. The sound of the arrows is the first thing the poem lets us hear of the god’s anger.

sentences.t: ὃ δ’ ἤϊε νυκτὶ ἐοικώς.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ēïe nykti eoikōs.
sentences.l: and he came, to night likened.
sentences.i: On he went, like the night.
sentences.n: ὃ δ’ ‘and he’ is the pronoun again, printed with a grave accent. ἤϊε is the epic imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, ‘he was going’. ἐοικώς, perfect participle of an old verb ‘be like’ (cf. ἔοικα), takes the dative νυκτί: ‘like night’. The simile is three words long, and the poet adds nothing to it.

sentences.t: ἕζετ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπάνευθε νεῶν, μετὰ δ’ ἰὸν ἕηκε·
sentences.tr: hezet’ epeit’ apaneuthe neōn, meta d’ ion heēke·
sentences.l: He sat then apart from the ships, and among them an arrow let fly;
sentences.i: Then he sat down away from the ships and let an arrow fly into their midst.
sentences.n: ἕζετ’ is ἕζετο, unaugmented imperfect of ἕζομαι ‘sit down’. ἀπάνευθε ‘far from’, with the genitive νεῶν. μετὰ … ἕηκε can be read as tmesis of μεθίημι ‘let go’, or with μετά as an adverb, ‘among them’; either way the arrow is loosed. ἕηκε is the epic aorist of ἵημι ‘send, let fly’, uncontracted. ἰόν ‘arrow’ is a different word from ἰός ‘poison, rust’.

sentences.t: δεινὴ δὲ κλαγγὴ γένετ’ ἀργυρέοιο βιοῖο·
sentences.tr: deinē de klangē genet’ argyreoio bioio·
sentences.l: and dread a clamour arose from the silver bow;
sentences.i: and a dread clang came from the silver bow.
sentences.n: δεινή ‘dread’ keeps the house rendering of δεινός. κλαγγή is a sharp, ringing noise, the noun of κλάζω (ἔκλαγξαν, 1.46). γένετ’ is γένετο, unaugmented aorist of γίγνομαι. ἀργυρέοιο βιοῖο: βιός ‘bow’ (accent on the last syllable) is a different word from βίος ‘life’, and both adjective and noun carry the epic genitive -οιο.

sentences.t:
οὐρῆας μὲν πρῶτον ἐπῴχετο καὶ κύνας ἀργούς,
αὐτὰρ ἔπειτ’ αὐτοῖσι βέλος ἐχεπευκὲς ἐφιεὶς
βάλλ’·
sentences.tr:
ourēas men prōton epōicheto kai kynas argous,
autar epeit’ autoisi belos echepeukes ephieis
ball’·
sentences.i: The mules were his first targets, and the swift dogs; then he loosed a sharp shaft at the men themselves and kept on striking.
sentences.n: οὐρῆας is the epic accusative plural of οὐρεύς ‘mule’. ἐπῴχετο, from ἐποίχομαι, ‘went at, attacked’. κύνας ἀργούς: ἀργός is ‘swift’ or ‘white, gleaming’, and which one is disputed; the house rendering is ‘swift’. ἐχεπευκής is usually taken as ‘sharp-pointed’; its formation is not certain. βάλλ’ is the imperfect βάλλε, ‘he kept shooting’, held back to the start of line 52 and stopped there by a pause.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δὲ πυραὶ νεκύων καίοντο θαμειαί.
sentences.tr: aiei de pyrai nekyōn kaionto thameiai.
sentences.l: and always pyres of the dead were burning, crowded-thick.
sentences.i: and all the while the pyres of the dead burned, crowded close together.
sentences.n: αἰεί is the epic form of ἀεί ‘always’. πυραί ‘pyres’ and νεκύων ‘of the dead’ (from νέκυς ‘corpse’). καίοντο is the unaugmented imperfect middle of καίω, ‘were burning’. θαμειαί ‘close-set, crowded’ stands last in the line: the pyres are many and close together.

sentences.t:
ἐννῆμαρ μὲν ἀνὰ στρατὸν ᾤχετο κῆλα θεοῖο,
τῇ δεκάτῃ δ’ ἀγορὴν δὲ καλέσσατο λαὸν Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
ennēmar men ana straton ōicheto kēla theoio,
tēi dekatēi d’ agorēn de kalessato laon Achilleus·
sentences.l:
For nine days throughout the army went the shafts of the god,
and on the tenth to assembly called the people Achilles;
sentences.i: For nine days the god’s shafts flew through the army; on the tenth, Achilles summoned the people to an assembly.
sentences.n: ἐννῆμαρ ‘for nine days’ is an adverb built on ἦμαρ ‘day’. κῆλα is a poetic word for the god’s shafts. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go, be gone’. τῇ δεκάτῃ ‘on the tenth’ (day understood). The second δέ in ἀγορὴν δέ is usually explained as apodotic δέ, picking up the time phrase τῇ δεκάτῃ; it need not be translated. καλέσσατο, aorist middle of καλέω with the doubled σ the metre allows.

sentences.t: τῷ γὰρ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη·
sentences.tr: tōi gar epi phresi thēke thea leukōlenos Hērē·
sentences.l: for in his mind it had put the goddess, white-armed Hera;
sentences.i: for the goddess, white-armed Hera, had put it into his mind.
sentences.n: τῷ is a pronoun, ‘to him’, and ἐπὶ φρεσί ‘in his mind’ (φρένες, the seat of thought). θῆκε is the unaugmented aorist of τίθημι ‘put’. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is Hera’s stock epithet, translated as the Odyssey translates it for mortal women. The poem often gives a god as the source of a man’s good idea, and the man still acts on it as his own.

sentences.t: κήδετο γὰρ Δαναῶν, ὅτι ῥα θνήσκοντας ὁρᾶτο.
sentences.tr: kēdeto gar Danaōn, hoti rha thnēskontas horato.
sentences.l: for she was troubled for the Danaans, because, dying, she saw them.
sentences.i: She cared for the Danaans, because she saw them dying.
sentences.n: κήδετο, from κήδομαι ‘care for, be troubled about’, takes the genitive Δαναῶν. ὅτι ‘because’. ῥα is an epic particle, ‘as it seems, you see’. ὁρᾶτο is the imperfect middle of ὁράω, used in the active sense ‘she saw’. θνήσκοντας ‘dying’ is the participle of the object understood (‘them’).

sentences.t:
οἳ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ἤγερθεν ὁμηγερέες τε γένοντο,
τοῖσι δ’ ἀνιστάμενος μετέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ epei oun ēgerthen homēgerees te genonto,
toisi d’ anistamenos metephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l:
And they, when they had gathered and assembled-together had become,
among them, standing up, spoke swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: When they had gathered and were all assembled, Achilles, swift of foot, stood up among them and spoke:
sentences.n: οἳ δ’ ‘and they’: the pronoun again, with a grave accent. ἤγερθεν is the epic aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’ (= ἠγέρθησαν), and ὁμηγερέες τε γένοντο ‘and had become assembled together’ is nearly the Odyssey’s line-ending (there ὁμηγερέες τ’ ἐγένοντο), and the English follows it. μετέφη, from μετάφημι ‘speak among’. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’: πόδας is an accusative of respect, and this is Achilles’ commonest epithet.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη νῦν ἄμμε παλιμπλαγχθέντας ὀΐω
ἂψ ἀπονοστήσειν, εἴ κεν θάνατόν γε φύγοιμεν,
εἰ δὴ ὁμοῦ πόλεμός τε δαμᾷ καὶ λοιμὸς Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē nyn amme palimplanchthentas oïō
aps aponostēsein, ei ken thanaton ge phygoimen,
ei dē homou polemos te damāi kai loimos Achaious·
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, I think we shall now be beaten back and go home again, if we escape death at all, since war and plague together are laying the Achaeans low.
sentences.n: ἄμμε is the Aeolic form of ἡμᾶς ‘us’. παλιμπλαγχθέντας ‘driven back off course’ is a compound of πάλιν ‘back’ and the aorist passive of πλάζω. ὀΐω ‘I think’ is an epic form of οἴομαι. ἀπονοστήσειν is a future infinitive, ‘will return home’. εἰ δή ‘if indeed’ comes close to ‘since’. δαμᾷ, future of δαμάζω ‘subdue’ (or present), takes both πόλεμος and λοιμός as subjects.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή τινα μάντιν ἐρείομεν ἢ ἱερῆα
ἢ καὶ ὀνειροπόλον, καὶ γάρ τ’ ὄναρ ἐκ Διός ἐστιν,
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē tina mantin ereiomen ē hierēa
ē kai oneiropolon, kai gar t’ onar ek Dios estin,
sentences.l:
But come now, some seer let us ask, or priest,
or even a dream-interpreter — for a dream too is from Zeus —
sentences.i: But come, let us ask some seer or priest, or even an interpreter of dreams, for a dream too comes from Zeus,
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ introduces a proposal. ἐρείομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive of ἐρέω ‘ask’, used as an exhortation: ‘let us ask’. μάντις ‘seer’, ἱερεύς ‘priest’ and ὀνειροπόλος ‘dream-interpreter’ are three kinds of people who could learn what a god wants. καὶ γάρ τ’ ‘for indeed’: epic τε here marks a general truth.

sentences.t:
ὅς κ’ εἴποι ὅ τι τόσσον ἐχώσατο Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
εἴτ’ ἄρ’ ὅ γ’ εὐχωλῆς ἐπιμέμφεται ἠδ’ ἑκατόμβης,
αἴ κέν πως ἀρνῶν κνίσης αἰγῶν τε τελείων
βούλεται ἀντιάσας ἡμῖν ἀπὸ λοιγὸν ἀμῦναι.
sentences.tr:
hos k’ eipoi ho ti tosson echōsato Phoibos Apollōn,
eit’ ar’ ho g’ euchōlēs epimemphetai ēd’ hekatombēs,
ai ken pōs arnōn knisēs aigōn te teleiōn
bouletai antiasas hēmin apo loigon amynai.
sentences.l:
who might tell why so greatly Phoebus Apollo is incensed,
whether then he finds fault over a vow or a hecatomb,
if perhaps of lambs’ savour and of goats’ full-grown
he wishes, having met it, from us the ruin to ward off.”
sentences.i: who could tell us why Phoebus Apollo is so incensed: whether he finds fault with us over a vow or a hecatomb, and whether, if he meets the savour of lambs and of full-grown goats, he may be willing to ward off ruin from us.”
sentences.n: εἴποι, optative in a relative clause with κ’ (κε = ἄν), ‘who might tell’. ἐχώσατο is the aorist of χώομαι ‘be incensed’. εὐχωλῆς and ἑκατόμβης are genitives of the cause of complaint: a vow not kept, a sacrifice not made. A hecatomb is a great sacrifice, nominally of a hundred oxen. αἴ κεν ‘if perhaps’ is the epic form of ἐάν. κνίσης ‘savour of burning fat’. ἀντιάσας ‘having met’ takes the genitive. ἀπὸ … ἀμῦναι is tmesis.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο·
sentences.tr: ētoi ho g’ hōs eipōn kat’ ar’ hezeto·
sentences.l: He then, having so spoken, sat down;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down;
sentences.n: ἤτοι, printed as one word in this edition (others print ἦ τοι), is a particle of affirmation, often barely translatable at the head of a formula. The line is the one the Odyssey uses to close a speech before another speaker rises, and its English is taken over: κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο is tmesis of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
Κάλχας Θεστορίδης οἰωνοπόλων ὄχ’ ἄριστος,
ὃς ᾔδη τά τ’ ἐόντα τά τ’ ἐσσόμενα πρό τ’ ἐόντα,
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ anestē
Kalchas Thestoridēs oiōnopolōn och’ aristos,
hos ēidē ta t’ eonta ta t’ essomena pro t’ eonta,
sentences.l:
and among them stood up
Calchas, Thestor’s son, of bird-diviners by far the best,
who knew the things that are and the things that will be and the things before that were,
sentences.i: and among them there stood up Calchas, son of Thestor, far the best of those who read the birds, who knew what is, what is to come, and what was before,
sentences.n: Θεστορίδης is a patronymic, ‘son of Thestor’. οἰωνοπόλος is one who reads the flight of birds (οἰωνός) for omens. ὄχ’ ἄριστος: ὄχα ‘by far’ strengthens the superlative. ᾔδη is the pluperfect of οἶδα, with the sense of a past ‘knew’. ἐόντα and ἐσσόμενα are the epic participles of εἰμί, present and future; πρό τ’ ἐόντα ‘things that were before’. The triple knowledge is the seer’s mark.

sentences.t:
καὶ νήεσσ’ ἡγήσατ’ Ἀχαιῶν Ἴλιον εἴσω
ἣν διὰ μαντοσύνην, τήν οἱ πόρε Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr:
kai nēess’ hēgēsat’ Achaiōn Ilion eisō
hēn dia mantosynēn, tēn hoi pore Phoibos Apollōn·
sentences.l:
and the ships he led of the Achaeans to Ilium
through his own seercraft, which to him granted Phoebus Apollo;
sentences.i: and he had guided the ships of the Achaeans to Ilium by his own gift of prophecy, which Phoebus Apollo had given him.
sentences.n: νήεσσ’ is the epic dative plural νήεσσι ‘ships’, with ἡγήσατ’ (ἡγέομαι ‘lead the way for’, + dative). Ἴλιον εἴσω ‘to Ilium’: εἴσω follows its noun. ἥν here is the possessive adjective ‘his own’, easily mistaken for the relative. μαντοσύνη ‘seercraft, prophetic skill’. τήν is the relative ‘which’, and οἱ ‘to him’ is an enclitic dative. πόρε is the unaugmented aorist ‘gave’.

sentences.t: ὅ σφιν ἐὺ φρονέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.tr: ho sphin ey phroneōn agorēsato kai meteeipen·
sentences.l: he, well-disposed in mind toward them, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: with kindly intent toward them he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: This whole line stands several times in the Odyssey, and its English is taken over unchanged. ὅ is the pronoun ‘he’. ἐὺ φρονέων is the uncontracted present participle (Attic εὖ φρονῶν), ‘thinking well, well disposed’. σφιν is the enclitic dative plural, ‘toward them’. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν is the fixed pair for opening a speech to an assembly.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ κέλεαί με Διῒ φίλε μυθήσασθαι
μῆνιν Ἀπόλλωνος ἑκατηβελέταο ἄνακτος·
sentences.tr:
ō Achileu keleai me Diï phile mythēsasthai
mēnin Apollōnos hekatēbeletao anaktos·
sentences.l:
“O Achilles, you bid me, dear to Zeus, to tell-out
the wrath of Apollo, the far-darting lord;
sentences.i: “Achilles, dear to Zeus, you bid me declare the wrath of Apollo, the far-darting lord.
sentences.n: Ἀχιλεῦ, the vocative, has single λ. κέλεαι is the uncontracted second person singular of κέλομαι ‘bid, urge’. Διῒ φίλε ‘dear to Zeus’ is a vocative phrase, with Διΐ the dative of Ζεύς. μυθήσασθαι ‘to tell out, declare’. μῆνιν is the poem’s first word again, now for Apollo. ἑκατηβελέταο ‘far-darting’, with the genitive -αο (= Attic -ου), is another epithet of the archer god, kept apart from ἑκηβόλος ‘far-shooting’.

sentences.t: τοὶ γὰρ ἐγὼν ἐρέω·
sentences.tr: toi gar egōn ereō·
sentences.l: Therefore I will speak;
sentences.i: So I will speak.
sentences.n: τοὶ γάρ, printed as two words in this edition, is the particle τοιγάρ ‘so then, therefore’; the τοι here is not the pronoun. ἐγών is the form of ἐγώ used before a vowel. ἐρέω is the epic uncontracted future of the verb that gives Attic ἐρῶ, ‘I will say’.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ σύνθεο καί μοι ὄμοσσον
ἦ μέν μοι πρόφρων ἔπεσιν καὶ χερσὶν ἀρήξειν·
sentences.tr:
sy de syntheo kai moi omosson
ē men moi prophrōn epesin kai chersin arēxein·
sentences.l:
but you, take heed, and to me swear
truly that you, ready, with words and with hands will aid me;
sentences.i: but you, mark this and swear to me that you will truly be quick to help me with words and with your hands.
sentences.n: σύνθεο is the aorist imperative middle of συντίθημι, ‘put together in your mind, take heed’. ὄμοσσον, aorist imperative of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’, with the doubled σ of epic verse. ἦ μέν is the formula of an oath, ‘truly’. πρόφρων ‘with a ready mind’ is an adjective used where English wants an adverb. ἀρήξειν, future infinitive of ἀρήγω ‘help, aid’, follows a verb of swearing.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ὀΐομαι ἄνδρα χολωσέμεν, ὃς μέγα πάντων
Ἀργείων κρατέει καί οἱ πείθονται Ἀχαιοί·
sentences.tr:
ē gar oïomai andra cholōsemen, hos mega pantōn
Argeiōn krateei kai hoi peithontai Achaioi·
sentences.l:
for truly I think I shall anger a man who greatly over all
the Argives rules, and him obey the Achaeans;
sentences.i: For I think I shall anger a man who holds great power over all the Argives, and whom the Achaeans obey.
sentences.n: ὀΐομαι, an epic form of οἴομαι ‘think’. χολωσέμεν is a future infinitive in -έμεν, ‘that I shall anger’. ὃς μέγα … κρατέει ‘who greatly rules over’, with the genitive Ἀργείων. Ἀργεῖοι ‘Argives’ is the second of Homer’s names for the army. καί οἱ πείθονται: οἱ is the enclitic dative ‘him’, after πείθομαι ‘obey’. Calchas does not yet name the man, though everyone knows whom he means.

sentences.t: κρείσσων γὰρ βασιλεὺς ὅτε χώσεται ἀνδρὶ χέρηϊ·
sentences.tr: kreissōn gar basileus hote chōsetai andri cherēï·
sentences.l: for stronger is a king when he is incensed with a man lower;
sentences.i: For a king has the upper hand when he is incensed with a lesser man.
sentences.n: κρείσσων, comparative of κρατύς, ‘stronger, mightier’. ὅτε with χώσεται, a short-vowel aorist subjunctive of χώομαι, makes a general statement, ‘whenever he is incensed’. χέρηϊ is the epic dative of χέρης ‘lesser, inferior’. The line is the first of three in which Calchas gives the rule of kings in the form of a proverb.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ τε χόλον γε καὶ αὐτῆμαρ καταπέψῃ,
ἀλλά τε καὶ μετόπισθεν ἔχει κότον, ὄφρα τελέσσῃ,
ἐν στήθεσσιν ἑοῖσι·
sentences.tr:
ei per gar te cholon ge kai autēmar katapepsēi,
alla te kai metopisthen echei koton, ophra telessēi,
en stēthessin heoisi·
sentences.i: For even if he digests his anger on the day itself, still he keeps his resentment afterwards in his breast until he has satisfied it.
sentences.n: εἴ περ … τε ‘even if’, with the subjunctive καταπέψῃ (καταπέσσω ‘digest’, literally ‘cook down’): the anger is swallowed and digested, but the grudge stays. χόλος is ‘anger’, κότος ‘resentment, grudge’; both are kept apart from μῆνις ‘wrath’. ἀλλά τε introduces the main clause, ‘yet’. ὄφρα τελέσσῃ ‘until he fulfils it’. ἑοῖσι ‘his own’ is the epic possessive (= ἑαυτοῦ).

sentences.t: σὺ δὲ φράσαι εἴ με σαώσεις.
sentences.tr: sy de phrasai ei me saōseis.
sentences.l: and you, consider whether you will keep me safe.”
sentences.i: So consider whether you will protect me.”
sentences.n: φράσαι is the aorist imperative middle of φράζω, ‘consider, take thought’. εἰ ‘whether’ introduces an indirect question with the future σαώσεις, from σαόω, the epic verb behind σῴζω ‘save, keep safe’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: This is the standing reply-formula, here with Achilles’ name and epithet in the second half of the line: τὸν δ’ ‘him’, the pronoun, as object of προσέφη ‘addressed’; ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’. It follows the English the Odyssey gives the same formula with Odysseus. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’, with πόδας an accusative of respect.

sentences.t: θαρσήσας μάλα εἰπὲ θεοπρόπιον ὅ τι οἶσθα·
sentences.tr: tharsēsas mala eipe theopropion ho ti oistha·
sentences.l: “Taking-courage fully speak the prophecy, whatever you know;
sentences.i: “Take courage, and tell us plainly the prophecy you know;
sentences.n: θαρσήσας is the aorist participle of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. μάλα ‘fully, very much’ goes with εἰπέ ‘speak’, the aorist imperative. θεοπρόπιον is ‘a prophecy, a message from a god’. ὅ τι οἶσθα ‘whatever you know’: οἶσθα is the second person singular of οἶδα.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὰ γὰρ Ἀπόλλωνα Διῒ φίλον, ᾧ τε σὺ Κάλχαν
εὐχόμενος Δαναοῖσι θεοπροπίας ἀναφαίνεις,
οὔ τις ἐμεῦ ζῶντος καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ δερκομένοιο
σοὶ κοίλῃς παρὰ νηυσί βαρείας χεῖρας ἐποίσει
συμπάντων Δαναῶν,
sentences.tr:
ou ma gar Apollōna Diï philon, hōi te sy Kalchan
euchomenos Danaoisi theopropias anaphaineis,
ou tis emeu zōntos kai epi chthoni derkomenoio
soi koilēis para nēusi bareias cheiras epoisei
sympantōn Danaōn,
sentences.l:
for no, by Apollo dear to Zeus, to whom you, Calchas,
praying, to the Danaans prophecies reveal,
no one, while I live and upon the earth am looking,
on you by the hollow ships heavy hands will lay
of all the Danaans,
sentences.i: For by Apollo, dear to Zeus, to whom you pray, Calchas, when you reveal prophecies to the Danaans, no one, while I live and look upon the earth, shall lay heavy hands on you beside the hollow ships — of all the Danaans, none,
sentences.n: οὐ μά with an accusative is the form of a negative oath, ‘no, by…’. ᾧ τε ‘to whom’, with epic τε. ἐμεῦ ζῶντος … δερκομένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘while I live and look’: to see the light is to be alive. Its second half and the phrase χεῖρας ἐποίσει ‘will lay hands on’ stand in the Odyssey too, and the English follows it. συμπάντων Δαναῶν depends on οὔ τις, ‘no one of all the Danaans’.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἢν Ἀγαμέμνονα εἴπῃς,
ὃς νῦν πολλὸν ἄριστος Ἀχαιῶν εὔχεται εἶναι.
sentences.tr:
oud’ ēn Agamemnona eipēis,
hos nyn pollon aristos Achaiōn euchetai einai.
sentences.l:
not even if Agamemnon you name,
who now by far the best of the Achaeans claims to be.”
sentences.i: not even if it is Agamemnon you name, who boasts that he is now far the best of the Achaeans.”
sentences.n: ἤν is the epic form of ἐάν ‘if’, with the subjunctive εἴπῃς. Achilles names the man Calchas would not. πολλόν is the epic form of πολύ, ‘by far’. εὔχεται is ‘claims, declares, boasts’: the same verb that means ‘pray’ at 1.87, and here it carries an edge.

sentences.t: καὶ τότε δὴ θάρσησε καὶ ηὔδα μάντις ἀμύμων·
sentences.tr: kai tote dē tharsēse kai ēuda mantis amymōn·
sentences.l: And then indeed took courage and spoke the seer, blameless:
sentences.i: And then the blameless seer took courage and spoke:
sentences.n: καὶ τότε δή ‘and then indeed’. θάρσησε is the unaugmented aorist of θαρσέω, answering Achilles’ θαρσήσας (1.85). ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’. μάντις ἀμύμων ‘the blameless seer’ follows the Odyssey; ἀμύμων is an old epithet whose exact meaning is not known, and the translation keeps ‘blameless’ every time.

sentences.t:
οὔ τ’ ἄρ ὅ γ’ εὐχωλῆς ἐπιμέμφεται οὐδ’ ἑκατόμβης,
ἀλλ’ ἕνεκ’ ἀρητῆρος ὃν ἠτίμησ’ Ἀγαμέμνων,
οὐδ’ ἀπέλυσε θύγατρα καὶ οὐκ ἀπεδέξατ’ ἄποινα,
τοὔνεκ’ ἄρ’ ἄλγε’ ἔδωκεν ἑκηβόλος ἠδ’ ἔτι δώσει·
sentences.tr:
ou t’ ar ho g’ euchōlēs epimemphetai oud’ hekatombēs,
all’ henek’ arētēros hon ētimēs’ Agamemnōn,
oud’ apelyse thygatra kai ouk apedexat’ apoina,
tounek’ ar’ alge’ edōken hekēbolos ēd’ eti dōsei·
sentences.i: “It is not a vow or a hecatomb that he faults, but his priest, whom Agamemnon dishonoured, refusing to release his daughter or accept the ransom: that is why the far-shooter has sent pains, and will send more.
sentences.n: Line 93 answers Achilles’ question of 1.65 in its own words, with οὐδ’ for ἠδ’. ἕνεκ’ ‘because of’, with the genitive ἀρητῆρος (1.11). ἠτίμησ’ is ἠτίμησε, the aorist of ἀτιμάω ‘dishonour’ (at 1.11 the poet used ἠτίμασεν from ἀτιμάζω). ἀπεδέξατ’, aorist of ἀποδέχομαι ‘accept’. τοὔνεκ’ is a crasis of τοῦ ἕνεκα, ‘for that reason’. ἑκηβόλος, used alone, is the god himself.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ὅ γε πρὶν Δαναοῖσιν ἀεικέα λοιγὸν ἀπώσει
πρίν γ’ ἀπὸ πατρὶ φίλῳ δόμεναι ἑλικώπιδα κούρην
ἀπριάτην ἀνάποινον, ἄγειν θ’ ἱερὴν ἑκατόμβην
ἐς Χρύσην·
sentences.tr:
oud’ ho ge prin Danaoisin aeikea loigon apōsei
prin g’ apo patri philōi domenai helikōpida kourēn
apriatēn anapoinon, agein th’ hierēn hekatombēn
es Chrysēn·
sentences.l:
and he will not, before, from the Danaans the unseemly ruin thrust away,
before to her dear father they give the quick-eyed maiden
unbought, unransomed, and lead a sacred hecatomb
to Chryse;
sentences.i: and he will not push the unseemly ruin away from the Danaans until the quick-eyed maiden goes back to her dear father, unbought and with no ransom, and a sacred hecatomb is led to Chryse.
sentences.n: πρίν … πρίν ‘before … before’ is the epic way of saying ‘not … until’. ἀπώσει, future of ἀπωθέω ‘thrust away’. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι (= δοῦναι). ἑλικῶπις is of disputed meaning, explained from ἕλιξ ‘turning’ as ‘with lively eyes’ or by others as ‘dark-eyed’; the house rendering is ‘quick-eyed’. ἀπριάτην ἀνάποινον ‘unbought, unransomed’. Χρύσην is the town again.

sentences.t: τότε κέν μιν ἱλασσάμενοι πεπίθοιμεν.
sentences.tr: tote ken min hilassamenoi pepithoimen.
sentences.l: then, having propitiated him, we might persuade him.”
sentences.i: Then we might appease him and win him over.”
sentences.n: τότε κεν with the optative πεπίθοιμεν, ‘then we might persuade’: κεν (= ἄν) marks the potential. πεπίθοιμεν is a reduplicated aorist optative of πείθω. μιν ‘him’ is the epic enclitic accusative. ἱλασσάμενοι, aorist participle middle of ἱλάσκομαι ‘propitiate, appease’, with the doubled σ of verse.
